title: The reverse test: do connected payees do better as a group?
question: Taking every payee of $1 million or more, do those with each kind of tie to decision-makers pass the Board faster, get more exceptions, or grow their share faster than like payees without it?
finding: 2,045 payees of $1 million or more were tested: 126 with campaign giving, 45 with lobbying contacts, 39 with a gift to paying staff, 8 with an add-back. Of 15 comparisons with enough payees, 1 differ from like payees by more than chance and 14 do not. Beyond chance: payees with lobbying contacts rank higher on years with an exception (position 58.8% against a chance range of 43.1% to 57.2%; 2.2 years on average against 1.1 years on average). No tie of any kind goes with a difference in: days to the Board’s final vote against like files; share of payments under no-competition rules; growth of its share of its main department’s spending. With this many comparisons one crossing of the 95% line is expected by chance alone.
how: Payees are grouped with like payees: the same size band of outside spending over the eight years (under $5 million, $5–25 million, $25–100 million, over $100 million) and the same kind (nonprofit or not). Within each group every payee is ranked on the outcome from 0% (lowest) to 100% (highest). "Position" is the average rank of the payees with the tie; 50% means no different from their like group. The chance range is where that average falls 95% of the time when the same number of payees is drawn at random from each group, 2,000 times. Board speed uses only payees with a timed file; share growth only payees paid by their main department in both fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2026.
limits: This is a comparison of groups and says nothing about any one payee. Size is controlled only in four bands, so a tie that goes with being large within a band, or with working in homelessness and health where the Board has waived bidding, will show as a difference without any favour being done. Ties are matched by exact name and are a floor. Sixteen comparisons are run, so one may cross the 95% line by chance alone. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. The $992.6 million of outside spending that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier is in none of the figures here; it is used only to tell that a payee is not new. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
